What makes these mosques especially fascinating is the way their architecture combines religious requirements, environmental adaptation, and older regional building traditions. The prayer spaces retained the essential mihrab orientation toward Mecca and square congregational plans, yet features such as monumental pinnacles, sculpted façades, checkerboard ornament, geometric motifs, and carefully controlled systems of indirect illumination reveal connections with surrounding West African architecture.  
 
The article even compares certain architectural forms with Dogon and Bobo houses, sanctuaries, and mosques, noting similarities in hollow cylindrical pillars, rooftop forms, and the symbolic organization of buildings. In several Futa Toro mosques, sunlight enters through carefully positioned openings and reflects across the curved surface of the mihrab, creating small areas of illumination inside otherwise dark interiors. Rather than viewing Sudano-Sahelian mosques as isolated religious structures, the article presents them as products of centuries of interaction between Islam, local building knowledge, political history, climate, and indigenous West African concepts of architectural form and symbolism.

Source: African Arts, Vol. 26, No. 3, July 1993.

text:
One thing that fools me is how African architects, developers, and road constructors never build houses or roads that are suitable for the African climate. We live in a hot, tropical region. The sun beats down on us for most of the year. Yet we build houses with concrete blocks, small windows, no ventilation, no trees around, no grass, nothing. It is so appalling.

We copied Western architecture without thinking. We saw the glass buildings of New York, London, and Paris, and we decided that was the standard of progress. We forgot that those buildings were designed for cold climates. They trap heat inside because that is what you want in winter. But here, winter does not exist. Here, we need to let heat out, not trap it in.

So we built concrete boxes with tiny windows, painted them in heat absorbing colours, and called them modern. We surrounded them with asphalt and concrete, removed the trees, and wondered why our homes feel like ovens. Then we bought air conditioners, spent a fortune on electricity, and called it comfort. This is not progress. This is stupidity dressed in modernity.

Traditional African architecture understood the climate. Thick walls that kept heat out. High ceilings that let hot air rise. Large overhangs that provided shade. Open courtyards that allowed cross ventilation. Trees and grass that cooled the air around the home. We abandoned all of that for colonial aesthetics. Now we live in houses that make us sick. Poor ventilation leads to respiratory issues. Heat trapped inside causes fatigue and dehydration. Lack of greenery increases stress and reduces mental well being. 

Roads are no better. We lay asphalt that absorbs heat, builds up thermal mass, and radiates it back all night. We remove trees that could provide shade. Then we complain that the weather is getting hotter.

text:
How I Built My Own Personal AI Software Factory (And How You Can Too)

It started with me using these AI tools as a thinking partner to work through complex challenges. That progressed to using Claude Code to shape large, complex features and develop specifications for them in markdown, which then led to breaking those specifications down into discrete, small tasks I could tackle individually. That's what led to /cog-shape, the skill I now use to break down complexity and build out larger systems.

Normally, I'd take notes on a piece of paper on my desk or quickly dash off a title for a GitHub issue whenever I noticed something wrong or thought of an improvement. But as you know with AI, it's garbage in, garbage out: better input yields better outputs. So that's how /cog-capture was born. It creates high-quality GitHub issues that would consistently yield high-quality pull requests.

Both of these you can download and use for free. https://t.co/TaR7mNUay3 They're just markdown text files, and you can knock yourself out updating them, modifying them, and making them better. Though I'm pretty confident that you'll get great results out of the box.

Next I found myself in Cursor or Claude Code building a feature, submitting the PR, and then getting the code review back and copying and pasting the review comments into my session where I had all the context for my changes. I thought, there's gotta be a better way. Using the gh command-line tool, I figured out a way to review the comments, compare them, make a decision about whether or not to fix them and how to respond, close the code review thread, and then update the PR as needed. This tool became cog respond.

This naturally led to cog revise, which, as you might expect, looks for code review feedback on any of my PRs, revises as needed and responds to the comments, and pushes changes up for re-review, fully autonomously. This shaved me hours each week alone.

At this point, I had about 1,000 hours working with these coding agents and was starting to get confident in their ability to autonomously build fully functional features or bug fixes without my intervention — as long as I had the product set up in a clean way where it could run all the tests and self-verify. With that setup, I got to a point where I could trust the system to complete an issue end-to-end. That led to cog build.

A note about the word cog: nobody wants to be a cog in the system, and all the things I'm automating are, in my opinion, the tedious, time-consuming, or annoying parts of software engineering. Where I like to spend my time isn't in the realm of handcrafted code (though I've spent a lot of time enjoying that space.) Where I like to spend my time and energy is in producing a product that actually helps people in the real world. That's the output of software engineering for me, and I like to spend my time at that higher level. All of this automation lets me do just that. The more I can push off to my team of cogs (as long as I'm not seeing a reduction in quality) the better.

Once I saw build working reliably, the result was a lot of PRs. Way more PRs authored and ready for my review than I was used to. At this point I still reviewed every PR and all of the code by hand, but once I approved a PR — (especially on projects where a squash merge were required) there was this dance of pulling the most recent code, integrating the merge with my pull request, resolving merge conflicts, retesting, pushing the changes, waiting for CI to complete successfully, and finally merging. With just 10 PRs in a single day, this dance could take as long as two hours to shepherd through to production. So cog merge was born to solve this problem and get those hours back each week. By my estimation, cog merge alone has saved me more than one day each week! It just works.

At this point, my trust in the system was such that I thought I could set up a fully automated software development lifecycle with each of these tools: pull an issue from the GitHub repository, build it, test it, push it up, revise when there was feedback to address, and then merge to get the code into production. 100% hands-free. So I built cog start to do this for me. It runs cog in a loop indefinitely. At first, I only had it do one issue at a time, then multiple issues, and finally I had it pulling any unassigned issue from my GitHub repository.

The net result was that all of a sudden, I had zero bugs in any of my repositories. As fast as I could use /cog-capture or /cog-shape to create issues, cog start would be running in the background on a $600 16GB Mac mini 24/7, pulling and resolving them. All I had to do was review and approve. This was mind-blowing for me. What was most humbling was how good the coding output was. Now, I care a lot about architecture, and I think I have a pretty decent one for my projects and I think that helps. I also have lots and lots of tests and guardrails in place, and I'm careful to make sure the issues I put into the system are small enough that I'm not asking it to do something impossible. But notwithstanding all of that, I now have a system that can produce as much as I describe, faster than I can think. If I can think it and describe it, it can build it 24/7. A single cog running all the time is probably 10x as productive as I am as a senior software engineer. To me, that's amazing.

Sometimes I have a lot of small, nitpicky bugs to fix, and when that happens, I've learned I can totally trust the system to solve them end-to-end without my intervention at all. So I added a feature called cog rubber-stamp that runs in the background and approves all of the PRs for me automatically, so they go through the entire system unattended. I labeled it "rubber-stamp" because the word has a kind of negative connotation, and I'm not sure this should be done all the time. In fact, most of the time I take the time to review the PRs. But I'm learning that, as good as these agents are getting, there are definitely times when I can rubber-stamp the PRs, go to sleep, and 20 issues just show up the next morning in production — all fixed, all perfect.

The next issue I was struggling with was the constant release of new coding models and coding harnesses. In my own personal experience, the harness really matters, and the LLM being used in the harness also really matters. To make it worse, I started to learn that these public coding benchmarks were being gamed and didn't actually represent my real-world experience. How am I to know what is the best tool for the job? So I built cog arena. Cog arena lets me route any issue to any collection of harness or model combos I choose in parallel. I have a judge model look at the output of all the attempts, take the best from each and build out a really high quality PR. This is great for high stakes issues but it's also been great to build intuition about which models and which harnesses work best for my code base specifically and not just some generalized coding benchmark.

A single cog takes up around 12 MB of RAM, so theoretically on my Mac mini I could have hundreds of cogs running in the background all the time picking up work and getting it done — but I ran into GitHub API limits, so I only run 35 cogs on my Mac mini. On my MacBook Pro, I spend my time exploring new ideas, shaping new product features, or capturing bugs and small feature requests. Then the Mac mini just goes to work.

The dev capacity on my Mac mini is easily 100 developers' worth of output, gated only by my ability to clearly architect and articulate what must be built, along with guidelines on how things should be put together. Because I have 25 years as a software engineer, I'm finding out this works really well for me. Maybe someone less experienced would do worse. I don't know. I know a lot of people say there's AI slop everywhere, and that not looking at the code guarantees you'll have a ball-of-mud architecture. But in my personal experience so far, this is working really clean and really well. If you can describe how you want your code to be in terms of functional and nonfunctional requirements, AI can do it most of the time, and that is a lot of leverage.

If that weren't enough, I've started adding to my system two cheap mini PCs — one running Linux and the other running Windows 11 Pro — both running cogs 24/7. 

Honestly, my problem now is one of multi-agent orchestration. I use a lightweight API call to lock and distribute tasks among the various machines, but mostly I'm trying to figure out how to keep them all busy all the time. It's really mind-blowing for me, and very exciting.

One important point in all of this: this whole system uses these AI coding harnesses in ways allowed by the various companies, so I can use their flat-rate plans. That means I'm using subsidized tokens and able to get an enormous amount of work done before I hit any of their limits. That said, newer open-source models are coming out, and I'm comparing their output with the closed-source models' output using cog arena so that if the costs become too high or the flat-rate pricing model disappear, I'll have something viable to move to. Long term, I'm seriously considering getting a server-class rack to run a very capable model locally and have all my cogs use it. At that point, I'll be able to build with effectively a multi-hundred-dev team for the cost of electricity.

If any of this is interesting to you, you can purchase Cog for $10 a month and have as many dev coding agents doing the software development lifecycle end-to-end as you have RAM. No per-usage charges, just a flat rate. 

I hope it helps a bunch of new software startups get off the ground, at a minimum. And I hope it helps small businesses generally do — in a more efficient and effective way — what I see a lot of people doing with their own claws: building custom software for themselves.

Did you know? That the royal palace in the city of Kano dates back to 1463-1499AD.
 
The 550-Year-Old Palace That's STILL a King's Home – Gidan Rumfa, Kano, Nigeria

You think Versailles or Buckingham Palace are ancient?
Meet Gidan Rumfa – the Emir’s Palace in Kano.
Built in the late 15th century (1463–1499) by Sarkin Muhammad Rumfa.
It’s the longest continuously occupied seat of power in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Over 550 years of unbroken royal authority. Still home to the Emir today.

Muhammad Rumfa wasn’t just a king – he was a visionary reformer.
The Kano Chronicle (one of Africa’s richest oral-written histories) credits him with 12 major innovations.
He expanded Kano’s legendary city walls, founded the massive Kurmi Market (still buzzing today), built the Juma’at Mosque, and created this palace as the new heart of the kingdom.
Evidence? Multiple historical sources, including accounts from North African scholar Al-Maghili, who personally advised Rumfa on governance and Islam.

Picture this in 1480s West Africa:
Rumfa ditches the old wooden palace for a massive new complex – Gidan Rumfa – on the city outskirts.
33–60 acres (sources vary, but it’s HUGE).
Surrounded by 20–30 ft high mud walls.
Inside: royal chambers, council halls, stables, mosques, gardens, audience rooms, and a labyrinth designed for defense and ceremony.
Classic Hausa architecture – intricate mud-brick, carved pinnacles (Zankwaye) still standing after 500+ years.

This wasn’t just a house. It was the nucleus of state power.
Rumfa introduced royal regalia: the long horn from Kanem-Bornu, ostrich-feather fans, the turban, and the tradition of prostrating before the king (inspired by Mali, Songhai, and Bornu empires).
He promoted capable slaves into high office and centralized administration.
Result? Kano became the wealthiest and most powerful Hausa city-state. Camel caravans poured in wealth.

Here’s the jaw-dropper:
Gidan Rumfa has survived everything.
Hausa kings → Fulani Jihad (early 1800s) → British colonial rule (1903) → modern Nigeria.
The Fulani kept it as the Emir’s seat. Parts were rebuilt, but the core and its role never changed.
No other palace in sub-Saharan Africa has held continuous authority this long.
(Source: Kano Emirate records & historians like Ibrahim Ado-Kurawa).

Today?
It’s still the official residence of the Emir of Kano – one of Africa’s most influential traditional rulers.
33+ acres of living history: schools, offices, mosques, and private quarters inside.
The Jahi ceremony (royal procession) still happens outside its gates, tracing directly back to Rumfa’s era.
Hausa ingenuity at its finest – mud architecture that has outlasted empires.

Why does this matter?
In an era when people downplay pre-colonial African achievements, Gidan Rumfa is living proof of sophisticated governance, urban planning, and architectural mastery in medieval West Africa.
It predates Columbus’s voyage. It outlasted the Ottoman and Mughal golden ages in continuity.
And it’s right here in Nigeria.

Next time you’re in Kano, this isn’t just a tourist spot – it’s a 550-year-old throne room still in use.
Respect the history. Respect the continuity. Respect African excellence.

text:
Hausa architecture demonstrates the philosophy of the Hausa man, and nothing portrays this better than the Courtyard (tsakar gida).

The tsakar gida reflects the value the Hausa place on family. Traditionally, a Hausa home was not built for a single nuclear family. It was built for generations. Brothers grew up together, got married, raised children, and continued living within the same compound. The courtyard became the social fabric that held everyone together.

It wasn't unusual for children to grow up surrounded by multiple fathers and mothers. Your father's brother was not simply an uncle—he was Baba. Your mother's sister was not simply an aunt—she was Mama. Those weren't just titles; they reflected how family responsibilities were shared. Children belonged to the household as much as they belonged to their biological parents.

But that philosophy did not stop at the walls of the house. The values cultivated inside the courtyard flowed into the wider society. The same spirit that made everyone inside the compound feel like one family also shaped the Hausa community beyond it. A child could travel hundreds of kilometres to another Hausa town for Islamic learning or trade and be welcomed into another household, not as a guest, but as a son. Kinship extended beyond blood. The house became the community, and the community became an extension of the house.

The architecture reinforced that way of life. Every room opened into the same courtyard. Children played together there. Elders gathered there. Families ate, celebrated, settled disputes, and lived their daily lives there. The design encouraged constant interaction while preserving the privacy of the home from the outside world.

It was also brilliant from an engineering perspective. The open courtyard improved airflow, brought natural light into every room, reduced heat, and created a comfortable living environment long before electricity or air conditioning.

Nothing in traditional Hausa architecture was accidental. Every wall, every room, every open space reflected the values of the people who built it. The embodied a philosophy of family, community, trust, privacy, and coexistence.

This is the inheritance many of us overlook. When we abandon our indigenous designs without first understanding the ideas embedded within them, we lose more than an architectural style. We gradually weaken the social fabric those designs helped nurture and replace it with ideas that were created for societies with different histories, different climates, and different ways of living.

There is nothing wrong with modernizing. But modernization should not require abandoning ourselves. We should improve what we inherited, not discard it. Because once a people lose the ideas woven into their own civilization, they eventually begin to lose the civilization itself.

text:
4. Hausa Compound Architecture and Dakali Vaulting
Northern Nigeria and Niger

Hausa compounds are organised around interconnected courtyards within a walled enclosure. Entry is through a covered reception vestibule called the zaure, which provides privacy from the street. Thick adobe walls. The dakali is a freehand vaulted ceiling technique unique to Hausa architecture, achieved without formwork by skilled plasterers working entirely by hand. Flat earth roof terraces used for sleeping and grain drying. The entire compound is organised around principles of privacy and spatial hierarchy.

Refinement: The dakali vaulted ceiling is one of the most technically sophisticated plasterwork traditions in West Africa and it is disappearing. It requires no imported materials and produces spaces with excellent acoustic and thermal properties. It deserves to be taught as a formal construction skill.

text:
That style actually came back from Brazil.
Freed Yoruba slaves returned from Bahia in the 1830s and many of them had trained there as master masons and carpenters. When they settled in Lagos, Abeokuta and Ibadan they built houses exactly like this one. We call them Aguda houses. Afro-Brazilian style.

 The arches carry the upper floor and let air move through the building. The railings on the balcony and fence were cut by hand, artisans back then made the finest patterns. That deep veranda is the reason the rooms stay cool without any AC 

Original Yoruba architecture was the courtyard compound. Mud walls around an open central court. Different thing entirely.
Most Aguda houses are rotting or getting knocked down for modern builds now.

🇩🇿 Standing near the city of Batna in Algeria and dating back to the 3rd century BCE, Madghacen is the oldest and most magnificent ancient royal mausoleum in North Africa, featuring a massive stone tumulus with a diameter of 58.9 meters and a height of 18.5 meters. 

Believed to have been built for the Numidian Kings, particularly King Madghis, this monumental structure presents a unique synthesis of traditional Berber/Amazigh architecture and Hellenistic influences with its surrounding 60 Doric columns. Symbolizing the engineering prowess and political might of the Numidian civilization long before Roman dominance, the mausoleum is currently on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List; however, despite facing a serious risk of collapse due to natural erosion and neglect, it continues to endure at the foothills of the Aures Mountains as the most powerful silent witness to the region's ancient history.

text:
I’m honestly surprised that this was the modern landscape surrounding the former capital of the Axumite Empire. I had always imagined a cityscape dominated by stone buildings and monumental architecture, but these photographs leave a very different impression. 

Much of the surrounding settlement appears to consist of clusters of circular earthen houses with thatched roofs, while the surviving stone architecture seems concentrated in churches, elite residences, defensive walls, and the monumental granite stelae that have endured for centuries.  

The contrast between these long-lasting ceremonial monuments and the far more perishable domestic architecture is striking. It makes me wonder how much the broader landscape around Axum actually changed after the decline of the empire. I have nothing against earthen architecture—in fact, earthen construction can be extraordinarily sophisticated and visually impressive—but I was surprised to see such a predominance of relatively simple earthen dwellings surrounding one of Africa’s greatest ancient capitals
not showing much high degree of intricate details and rich ornamentation like Hausa or  Ndebele earthen architecture or neighbouring Yemen.

These photographs also raise an interesting question about how ancient Axum may have appeared. If a substantial proportion of ordinary residences surrounding Axum   were constructed from earth, timber, and thatch, they would have left far fewer archaeological traces than stone palaces, churches, tombs, and the famous granite obelisks. That would help explain why the archaeological record is dominated by monumental stone architecture, while the earthen homes of the majority of the population from the looks of things look very dull.  

 At the same time, archaeology confirms that ancient Axum possessed impressive stone palaces and elite buildings, so these twentieth-century photographs should not be taken as a direct reconstruction of the ancient city. They do, however, make me wonder whether much of the urban fabric surrounding Axum’s monumental core consisted primarily of earthen architecture resembling this seen in image 1.

I think what surprised me most is that this is the landscape where the capital of the Axumite Kingdom once stood. I expected something closer to Timbuktu, where more elaborate residential architecture dominated the landscape not just restricted to the elites across a broader portion of the city rather than monumental stone architecture being concentrated primarily in elite, religious, and ceremonial contexts.  

 Whether that expectation is accurate is another question because I have more studying to consider, but these images certainly challenged the mental picture I had of Axum.

text:
A courtyard house that cools itself with rainwater, saves timber by refusing veneer, and still manages to look like it’s always been there.

Studio Amoeba built it around two courtyards, connected by a single swing that faces either way. Basalt steps and stone floors keep the carbon footprint down. The wooden ceiling is plain plywood, polished directly, no veneer, saving timber without losing warmth. In summer, water sprinkled on the brick courtyard floor cools the air the way a clay pot cools water.

The land has been in the family for generations. The design team treated that history like a material, choosing toggle switches and hand-woven textiles over anything that reads as new.

Most architects design homes to stand out. This one was built to disappear beside its neighbours.

House Around the Two Courtyards | Studio Amoeba, Pashmin Shah & Satyajeet Patwardhan

text:
Your nose finds the smell of rain at five parts per trillion. That is one drop in twenty Olympic pools, a lower detection limit than a shark has for blood in water. We evolved that sensitivity to locate water. Then we built houses engineered to remove it.

The molecule is geosmin, made by Streptomyces bacteria living in soil. Through a dry spell the bacteria keep producing it while plant oils leach out and settle into clay and porous stone. The ground loads up like a battery.

Rain discharges it. MIT filmed the exact moment in 2015 with high speed cameras across 38 surfaces, 16 soils and 12 engineered materials. When a drop lands on something porous it traps air bubbles at the point of contact. The bubbles shoot up through the flattening drop like champagne and burst, throwing hundreds of aerosol droplets into the air in a few microseconds. Those aerosols carry the geosmin and the oils. That spray is the entire delivery system.

Two conditions have to hold. Porous surface, light rain. A downpour hits too fast for bubbles to form inside the droplet, which is why a drizzle smells stronger than a storm.

Now consider what sits within thirty feet of most front doors. Asphalt, concrete, sealed pavers, treated decking. None of it absorbs plant oils and none of it is permeable enough to make bubbles. The chemistry never loads and the physics never fires.

Then the walls. Older homes leaked close to a full air change an hour through gaps around windows, doors and floorboards. Tight modern construction runs 0.35 or lower, and the air that does come in gets pulled through a filter whose entire purpose is capturing suspended particles. Petrichor is a suspended particle.

A courtyard house beats both problems by accident. Open ground inside the building footprint, unglazed tile and soil that stay porous, no barrier between wet earth and living room. The smell has ten feet to travel and nothing to travel through.

Evolution spent a few hundred thousand years tuning us to five parts per trillion. Energy codes took about fifty to engineer it back out.

text:
5. Tunisia
Medina of Tunis, Ksar Ghilane Troglodyte Architecture, Djerba Houch Courtyard Houses

The Medina of Tunis, UNESCO World Heritage since 1979, contains over 700 monuments built between the 7th and 19th centuries, including mosques, mausoleums, palaces and fountains. The urban fabric follows the same human-scale logic as the Moroccan medinas, with narrow covered streets designed to maximise shade and minimise solar heat gain at street level.

The troglodyte houses of Matmata in southern Tunisia are dug vertically into the soft rock of the plateau. An open circular courtyard is excavated first, then rooms are carved horizontally into the courtyard walls. The underground temperature remains between 20 and 22 degrees Celsius year-round regardless of surface temperatures that can exceed 45 degrees in summer. The film Star Wars used Matmata as a filming location in 1976.

The traditional houch of Djerba Island is a courtyard house with thick limestone walls, a single entrance door and rooms arranged around a central courtyard. The same inward-facing spatial logic as the Moroccan riad, adapted to the island’s coastal climate.

Refinement potential: The Matmata troglodyte house is one of the most extreme passive cooling solutions in North Africa and one of the least studied. Digging into the earth rather than building on top of it produces consistent interior temperatures that no mechanical system can match at the same cost. It deserves formal architectural study and contemporary application in extreme heat contexts across the Sahel.

text:
3. Morocco
Riad Courtyard Houses, Kasbah Rammed Earth Fortresses, Medina Urban Planning, Zellij Tilework

The Moroccan riad is a private courtyard house organised entirely inward, with all rooms opening onto a central garden courtyard rather than the street. The courtyard provides shade, natural ventilation and privacy simultaneously. All windows face inward. The street-facing wall is blank. This is not poverty of design. It is a deliberate climate and privacy strategy that has been refined over a thousand years.

The Kasbahs of the Atlas Mountains and the Draa Valley, including Ait Benhaddou, UNESCO World Heritage since 1987, are rammed earth fortresses built using the pisé technique: earth mixed with straw and lime, compacted in formwork and left to cure. Walls up to a metre thick, ornamented with geometric relief work, have survived centuries of heat and rain. The Medinas of Fez and Marrakesh are human-scale urban masterpieces of narrow shaded streets, covered souks and communal nodes that keep ground level temperatures measurably lower than the open boulevards built alongside them during the colonial period. Zellij, hand-cut geometric tilework, and carved stucco finish interior surfaces with a craft tradition that has been passed between master craftsmen for over 800 years.

Refinement potential: The riad courtyard and the pisé rammed earth kasbah are two of the most climate-appropriate building systems in North Africa, both being refined into contemporary hospitality and residential architecture right now. The Medina urban planning principle, narrow streets, covered passages, human scale, produces passive cooling that modern urban planning in Morocco’s new cities entirely ignores.

કોણ છે સોનમ વાંગચુક અને કેટલું ભણેલા છે?

તેમની સૌથી ખાસ વાત એ છે કે તેમણે પ્રારંભિક શિક્ષણ કોઈ મોટી સ્કૂલમાંથી નહીં, પણ પોતાના ઘરે જ મેળવ્યું હતું. એક નાનકડા ગામડા માંથી નીકળીને તેમણે NIT શ્રીનગર સુધીની સફર નક્કી કરી અને ત્યાંથી એન્જિનિયરિંગની ડિગ્રી મેળવી. બાદમાં તેઓ હાયર એજ્યુકેશન માટે વિદેશ પણ ગયા.

સોનમ વાંગચુકનો જન્મ વર્ષ 1966માં લદ્દાખના અલ્ચી પાસેના એક નાનકડા ગામમાં થયો હતો. તે સમયે તેમના ગામમાં કોઈ સ્કૂલ નહોતી. આ જ કારણે તેઓએ 9 વર્ષની ઉંમર સુધી કોઈ સ્કૂલમાં અભ્યાસ કર્યો નહોતો. તેમને પ્રારંભિક શિક્ષણ તેમની માતાએ ઘરે જ તેમની માતૃભાષામાં આપ્યું હતું. આ દરમિયાન તેઓ વાંચવા-લખવાનું શીખ્યા અને પાયાનું શિક્ષણ મેળવ્યું.

NIT શ્રીનગરથી કર્યું મિકેનિકલ એન્જિનિયરિંગ - શાળાકીય શિક્ષણ પૂર્ણ કર્યા પછી સોનમ વાંગચુકે તે સમયના રીજનલ એન્જિનિયરિંગ કોલેજ, શ્રીનગર (હવે નેશનલ ઇન્સ્ટિટ્યુટ ઓફ ટેક્નોલોજી – NIT શ્રીનગર)માં એડમિશન લીધું. તેઓએ વર્ષ 1987માં મિકેનિકલ એન્જિનિયરિંગમાં BTechની ડિગ્રી મેળવી હતી..

- એન્જિનિયરિંગ પછી સોનમ વાંગચુકે ફ્રાન્સના ક્રેટેરે સ્કૂલ ઓફ આર્કિટેક્ચર, ગ્રેનોબલમાંથી અર્થન આર્કિટેક્ચર (Earthen Architecture)નો અભ્યાસ કર્યો. આ કોર્સમાં તેઓએ એવા ઘરો બનાવવાની ટેકનિક શીખી, જે પર્યાવરણને અનુકૂળ હોય અને પહાડી વિસ્તારોની જરૂરિયાતો અનુસાર તૈયાર કરી શકાય

લદ્દાખમાં વર્ષ 1988માં સ્ટુડન્ટ્સ એજ્યુકેશનલ એન્ડ કલ્ચરલ મૂવમેન્ટ ઓફ લદ્દાખ (SECMOL)ની સ્થાપના કરી. આ સંસ્થાએ લદ્દાખના સરકારી સ્કૂલોમાં શિક્ષણની ગુણવત્તા સુધારવા માટે અનેક મહત્વની પહેલ કરી છે.

તેઓએ આઇસ સ્તૂપ (Ice Stupa) જેવી ટેકનિક વિકસાવી, જે પાણીને બરફના સ્વરૂપમાં સંગ્રહિત રાખીને ઉનાળામાં ખેતી માટે ઉપલબ્ધ કરાવે છે. આ ઉપરાંત, તેઓએ હિમાલયન ઇન્સ્ટિટ્યુટ ઓફ અલ્ટરનેટિવ્સ, લદ્દાખ (HIAL)ની સહ-સ્થાપના કરી, જ્યાં વિદ્યાર્થીઓને અનુભવ આધારિત શિક્ષણ આપવા પર ભાર મૂકવામાં આવે છે.

मैं कॉकरोच जानता पार्टी का समर्थक बिल्कुल नहीं - मगर सोनम वांगचुक इस देश की एक बहुत ही दुर्लभ बिरले प्रतिभाओं में से हैं- एक नज़र इस सख्स की शख़्सियत पर।

1- लद्दाख में शिक्षा क्रांति – 1988 में SECMOL (Students’ Educational and Cultural Movement of Ladakh) की स्थापना कर शिक्षा व्यवस्था में बड़ा बदलाव लाया। 

2- आइस स्तूप (Ice Stupa) के आविष्कारक – कृत्रिम ग्लेशियर विकसित किए, जो सर्दियों में पानी को बर्फ के रूप में संचित करते हैं और गर्मियों में किसानों को सिंचाई के लिए पानी उपलब्ध कराते हैं। Swiss ऐल्प्स में यूरोप का पहला आइस स्तूप स्थापित किया।

3- सौर ऊर्जा आधारित भवन – लद्दाख जैसे अत्यधिक ठंडे क्षेत्र में बिना जीवाश्म ईंधन के सौर ऊर्जा से गर्म रहने वाले भवन विकसित किए। 

4- पर्यावरण एवं सतत विकास – जलवायु परिवर्तन, टिकाऊ वास्तुकला और स्थानीय संसाधनों पर आधारित विकास के लिए अंतरराष्ट्रीय स्तर पर पहचान बनाई। 

5- 3 इडियट्स’ से प्रेरणा – आमिर खान द्वारा निभाया गया फुंसुख वांगडू का किरदार काफी हद तक सोनम वांगचुक के जीवन और कार्यों से प्रेरित माना जाता है। 

प्रमुख Awards:

1- रेमन मैग्सेसे पुरस्कार (2018) – शिक्षा सुधार और सामुदायिक विकास के लिए एशिया के सबसे प्रतिष्ठित सम्मानों में से एक।
2- Rolex Award for Enterprise (2016) – Ice Stupa नवाचार के लिए। 
3- Global Award for Sustainable Architecture (2017) – सतत एवं पर्यावरण-अनुकूल वास्तुकला में योगदान के लिए। 
4- International Terra Award (2016) – मिट्टी आधारित टिकाऊ निर्माण (Earthen Architecture) के लिए। 
5- CNN-IBN Real Heroes Award (2008) – समाज में उत्कृष्ट योगदान के लिए। 
6- Ashoka Fellowship (2002) – सामाजिक उद्यमिता के लिए। 
7- The Green Teacher Award (2004) – पर्यावरण शिक्षा में योगदान के लिए। 
8- Governor’s Medal (1996) – जम्मू-कश्मीर में शिक्षा सुधार के लिए। 
9- Honorary Doctor of Letters (D.Litt.), Symbiosis International University (2018) – शिक्षा और समाज सेवा में योगदान के लिए मानद उपाधि। 

ऐसे लोग देश की धरोहर होते हैं।

" Sonam Wangchuk has been on a hunger strike for over 18 days " 

But not a single Media channel covering this

He is great engineer , activist, innovator, education reformer, and environmentalist

His biggest achievements -

- Started SECMOL (Students' Educational and Cultural Movement of Ladakh), where students learn by doing real projects instead of only reading books.

- Invented the Ice Stupa, a cone-shaped tower of ice that stores water in winter so farmers have water in spring.

- Built schools and buildings that stay warm naturally, using sunlight instead of expensive heaters.

- Solar-Heated Tents – He helped develop lightweight solar-heated tents for people working in extremely cold Himalayan regions, including the Indian Army.

He have got alot of awards in world -

> Ramon Magsaysay Award (2018) - Often called "Asia's Nobel Prize."

> Rolex Award for Enterprise (2016) - One of the world's most competitive innovation awards.

> Global Award for Sustainable Architecture (2017) - International architecture award for pioneers in sustainable design.

> International Terra Award (2016) - International award recognizing excellence in earthen architecture.

Sonam Wangchuk has given a lot to India, and I think there are very few people in India who have contributed this much to the country. Right now, he is a true gem.

Seeing him on a hunger strike while almost no one is paying attention makes me sad because he has inspired me a lot. Whenever I look at his ideas, they inspire me to be a better person.

He is on a hunger strike because he wants the Education Minister to resign. Due to this minister, there have been many exam paper leaks in India, and there has been no accountability. This is not happening for the first time it has been happening for the last 4-5  years. That is why he wants the Education Minister to resign.

I don't know what our government is doing. It has been 18 days, and no one is paying attention or covering this news. 

It makes me very sad to see this, but I stand with  . I just hope this issue is resolved as soon as possible. 

Maybe God will give me the strength to deal with this.

text:
Africa is home to some of the most incredible biodiversity on Earth, which has inspired countless forms of biomimicry for centuries. 

Pre-colonial African builders didn’t just copy nature, they built in harmony with it, creating climate-responsive and truly sustainable structures long before the term existed.

The Nest at Sossusvlei is a beautiful modern refinement of that ancient knowledge: modeled after the massive sociable weaver nests, with double-skin walls, natural ventilation and zero air-conditioning in one of the harshest deserts. It’s not reinventing the wheel, it’s a homecoming to wisdom our ancestors already mastered (think Musgum shell houses, Zulu beehive huts or the incredible thermal regulation of Djenné’s earthen architecture).

As I’ve always said, Africa has enormous potential for architectural tourism rooted in this deep relationship with nature. We’re sitting on a goldmine of inspiration, but we’re still not fully leveraging it. Time to change that.

5. Rwanda
Rugo Compound Architecture, Terraced Agriculture Settlements,  Muyinga Library

Traditional Rwandan homesteads, the rugo, consisted of a circular compound enclosed by a woven sorghum stalk fence, with cone-roofed dwellings of wattle and daub arranged around a central cattle pen. The cone roof uses a double-layer thatch system that insulates against both heat and heavy equatorial rainfall. The University of Rwanda has included vernacular architecture in its architecture syllabus, one of the few institutions on the continent to do so formally.

The Muyinga Library, a contemporary project built from locally sourced compressed earth blocks for a school for deaf children, is one of the strongest examples of vernacular material intelligence applied to contemporary social infrastructure in East Africa.

Refinement potential: Rwanda’s post-genocide reconstruction was done almost entirely in imported concrete block without reference to any local traditions. The rugo compound spatial logic, a protected inner space surrounded by separate functional structures, is directly applicable to contemporary community housing design. The Muyinga Library proves it is already happening.

2. Kenya
Swahili Coral Stone Architecture, Lamu Old Town, Gedi Ruins, Thimlich Ohinga Stone Fortress

Lamu Old Town is the oldest and best-preserved Swahili settlement in East Africa, founded before the 14th century and continuously inhabited since. Buildings are constructed in fossilised coral stone and mangrove timber. Coral was quarried locally, cut into blocks and laid with lime mortar mixed with red earth. The walls provide natural thermal mass against coastal heat. Houses are built around a central courtyard called the kiwanda, with screened wooden balconies for ventilation and privacy, and intricately carved doors signalling social status. UNESCO World Heritage since 2001.

The Gedi Ruins in coastal Kenya are the remains of a medieval Swahili town featuring stone houses, mosques, a palace and ancient wells, abandoned in the 17th century and still structurally coherent enough to read the spatial logic of the settlement. Thimlich Ohinga in the Lake Victoria basin is a 16th century dry-stone granite fortress whose construction technique, large stones dry-laid without mortar into curving enclosure walls, directly parallels Great Zimbabwe.

Refinement potential: The Swahili coral stone and carved door traditions are being replaced by cement and aluminium in Lamu. The courtyard house spatial logic, cross ventilation, shade and privacy solved simultaneously in one layout, is directly applicable to contemporary coastal residential and hospitality design. Architects like Urko Sanchez have already demonstrated this in Mombasa

meta muse spark 1.1 vs gpt 5.6 sol vs fable 5 vs grok 4.5

meta recently dropped muse spark 1.1 – a multimodal reasoning model from meta superintelligence labs built for agentic tasks. key facts:

• 1m token context with active self-management – the model compacts its own history and keeps only the steps needed for later work

• trained to orchestrate multi-agent systems: as main agent it plans and delegates to parallel subagents, as subagent it sticks to its job and knows when to escalate back

• computer use trained to pick between scripting and clicking – writes automation when it's faster, clicks when it's simpler, batches actions per step

• first public api from meta: the meta model api is now in preview

• benchmarks: sweeps the agent column – mcp atlas 88.1 (opus 4.8: 82.2), jobbench 54.7 (opus: 48.4), humanity's last exam 62.1 (1st). loses coding – deepswe 1.1 53.3 vs gpt 5.5's 67.0, swe bench pro 61.5 vs opus's 69.2

our test – 3 prompts, single-file html, three.js, fully procedural, no assets:

1. norwegian house cantilevered over a fjord in a snowstorm – transmissive glass wall, fully modelled interior
2. beijing siheyuan courtyard house in dawn fog – instanced roof tiles, dougong brackets, glowing paper windows
3. new mexico adobe pueblo in an approaching dust storm – deep window reveals, windward grit accumulation

we ran the test on  platform

results:

- cost
#1 muse spark 1.1 – $0.20
#2 grok 4.5 – $0.51
#3 gpt 5.6 sol – $1.93
#4 fable 5 – ~$5.20

- output tokens
#1 muse spark 1.1 – 41,868
#2 gpt 5.6 sol – 49,139
#3 grok 4.5 – 64,954
#4 fable 5 – 81,849

- lines of code
#1 muse spark 1.1 – 1,799
#2 gpt 5.6 sol – 2,377
#3 fable 5 – 3,088
#4 grok 4.5 – 4,216

observations:

• muse spark is the cheapest of the four by a wide margin – 2.5x under grok, ~26x under fable per run. output quality tracks the price

• only 7.4% of its output tokens are reasoning (3,104 of 41,868) – the model barely thinks before writing. economic, not pedantic: it commits to the first plan and ships it

• the low loc is not compression, it's omission – all three prompts demanded instancing, muse spark delivered it in one

muse spark's code quality – reviewed by fable 5:

upsides: 
1. all three files run
2. the adobe grit effect is legit – shader injection via onbeforecompile, windward faces detect storm direction through a normal-dot-wind term and darken procedurally
3. the fjord glass is real meshphysicalmaterial with transmission and ior, not a transparent quad
4. the siheyuan properly instances barrel tiles, dougong blocks and courtyard pavers

downsides: 
1. in the fjord file the strafe vector is negated – press a, you move right; press d, you move left. exactly the key mix-up we kept hitting with this model
2. all three files ship the model's self-doubt as comments: "// actually yaw orientation: need correct" sits above a direction vector that gets computed, abandoned and recomputed – dead vectors allocated every frame, 60 times a second
3. the siheyuan registers two separate keydown listeners, one containing an empty if-block
4. snow "accumulation" on the norway roof is a sine wobble on a scale value, not accumulation
5. "instanced snow" became 3,500 plain points. zero dispose calls anywhere

pattern: minimal reasoning, minimal code, minimal price. it nails the flashy requirements – shaders, transmissive glass – and quietly drops the boring ones: instancing, controls, cleanup. you get a demo that mostly runs and a control scheme you can't trust

text:
Oualata, Mauritania — a masterpiece of Saharan earthen architecture and women’s mural traditions. In this ancient caravan city of the Adrar region, reddish earth walls are transformed with bold white geometric and curvilinear designs, framing doors, alcoves, stairways, and domestic interiors with striking visual rhythm.

Founded in the 12th century as a desert caravan stopover, Oualata became part of Mauritania’s remarkable Saharan urban heritage alongside Chinguetti, Tichitt, and Ouadane. Its decorated homes show how architecture, ornament, identity, and daily life merge into one powerful artistic tradition.

MoMA has released an 11-minute-51-second video essay worth your time: Martino Stierli, the museum’s chief curator of architecture and design, takes viewers inside independence-era modernist buildings featured in “Architects of Liberation: Modernism in Western Africa.” 

The exhibition covers Benin, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal and Togo, and is on view at MoMA in New York City from 5 July 2026 to 2 January 2027.

There is a larger media conversation happening here. 

German broadcaster Deutsche Welle (DW) has released the 55-minute documentary “The Red and the Grey Matter: New Architecture in Africa,” while the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s “Africa’s Cultural Landmarks” comprises 12 short documentaries filmed at sites across sub-Saharan Africa between 2022 and 2024 and released online in 2025. 

Museums and broadcasters are investing in original location filming about African architecture, heritage and the people responsible for preserving and rethinking these spaces. Something worth tracking.

text:
At its height in the 14th century, the Mali Empire controlled territory stretching across a significant portion of West Africa, encompassing parts of modern-day Mali, Senegal, Guinea, Niger, and several other nations — an empire larger than Western Europe at the time.
Its most famous city, Timbuktu, became one of the medieval world's most important centers of trade, scholarship, and Islamic learning. By the time of Mansa Musa's reign, Timbuktu housed multiple universities and an estimated 700,000 to a million manuscripts in its libraries — covering subjects ranging from astronomy and mathematics to law, medicine, and Islamic theology. Scholars traveled from across the Islamic world specifically to study and teach in Timbuktu's institutions.
The empire's wealth came primarily from controlling crucial trans-Saharan trade routes connecting sub-Saharan Africa's gold-producing regions to North African and Mediterranean markets. Mali essentially controlled the supply chain for a substantial portion of the gold that circulated throughout the medieval Islamic world and, indirectly, medieval Europe.
Mansa Musa, recognizing the value of scholarship as both a religious obligation and a source of prestige, brought back architects, scholars, and books from his pilgrimage to Mecca, commissioning the construction of the famous Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, which still stands today as one of the most significant examples of Sudano-Sahelian architecture in the world.
Despite this scale of wealth, scholarship, and architectural achievement, the Mali Empire and figures like Mansa Musa remain significantly less prominent in popular global historical narratives compared to contemporaneous European, Middle Eastern, or East Asian powers of similar scale and influence — a gap that historians attribute partly to historical Eurocentric scholarship and partly to the empire's eventual decline and absorption by successor states.

text:
How Traditional Nigerian Architecture Solved Problems Modern Buildings Create 🧵

Many modern Nigerian buildings spend money solving problems traditional architecture already solved.
-Cooling.
-Ventilation.
-Community.
-Climate response.

Traditional Nigerian homes were built for the weather, not for Instagram. Courtyards, verandas, shaded walkways, and thick walls all helped regulate temperature naturally.

Modern apartments often depend on air conditioning because many designs ignore cross-ventilation and solar orientation.

The building fights the climate instead of working with it.

Traditional compounds encouraged airflow from multiple directions.

Many contemporary developments have rooms with only one small window and limited natural ventilation.

Traditional architecture also understood community.

Shared courtyards created social interaction, passive surveillance, and stronger neighbourhood bonds.

Local materials such as earth and laterite often provided excellent thermal performance long before sustainability became a global buzzword.

The lesson is not that we should stop building modern structures. The lesson is that modern architecture should learn from indigenous intelligence.

The smartest buildings of the future may look forward by looking backward.

Nigeria has architectural lessons worth preserving.

Project Overview 

This project is conceived as an architectural interpretation of the call to prayer.... a universal call across religions, inviting reflection, worship, and spiritual connection. Rather than referencing a single faith, the design abstracts prayer as a radiating expression, communicated through form, light, and movement.

Design Highlights

1. Form inspired by the geometry of horns and ladder rungs, symbolizing a call to worship and ascension

2. Building mass begins grounded and focused, then expands outward to symbolize prayer extending to the collective realm

3. Central dome envisioned as a symbolic covering for all peoples, representing unity, protection, and shared spiritual belonging

4. Central monument as a landmark supported by interconnected spaces for prayer, meditation, and quiet reflection

5. Design prioritizes inclusivity, clarity of circulation, universal accessibility, user comfort, and calm contemplative experience

Project Details

- Location: Africa
- Architect: The Building Practice
- Typology: Multi-religious monument

text:
Pritzker Prize-winning architect Diébédo Francis Kéré  argues that African architecture must stop copying Western models and instead engage the real needs of its people and environment.

Born in Gando, Burkina Faso — where over 80% of the population cannot read or write — Kéré returned from his architecture studies in Berlin to build with his community, not for them.

His Gando Primary School, constructed entirely by local villagers using clay and handmade bricks, demonstrates that low-cost building can be high-quality design.

From teacher housing to the National Park of Mali, Kéré's practice proves that architecture born from local knowledge, community participation, and environmental responsiveness is stronger than any imported model.

text:
Copy-Paste Architecture: Are We Designing or Replicating?

There’s a quiet shift happening in Lagos’ built environment. We are no longer designing buildings.
We are replicating them.Walk through Lekki, Ikoyi, Ajah.
-Same glass фасades.
-Same box forms.
-Same “modern luxury” aesthetic.
-Different plots. Same buildings.

This is what I call Copy-Paste Architecture.

Pre-designed templates reused across multiple developments with minimal contextual adaptation.

Why is it happening?
-Speed to market
-Cost efficiency
-Social media influence
-Weak demand for originality

But here’s the issue:
-Lagos is not London.
-It is not Dubai.
-Yet many buildings here behave like they are.

The consequences:
-Poor ventilation
-Heat retention
-Flood vulnerability
-High maintenance costs

Beyond performance, there’s a deeper loss:
Identity.
Cities should have character. We are building visual monotony and let’s be clear, this is systemic.

Clients want familiar aesthetics.
Developers want quick ROI.
Design is treated as optional.

But architecture is not just about looks.
It is strategy.
It is climate response.
It is human experience.

If we continue like this, Lagos risks becoming a city of copies with no original voice.

The solution?
-Context-driven design.
-Local materials.
-Climate intelligence.
-Intentional creativity.
Because if everything can be copied…

Then nothing is truly designed.

text:
Today, 1 August, Benin marks 66 years of independence. It is the only African country with an independence anniversary on this date, and this small West African country matters far more than its size suggests.

Independence came in 1960 from France. The country was called the Republic of Dahomey at the time. Hubert Maga was its first president. The name Benin arrived in 1975, taken from the Bight of Benin off its coast.

Before colonization, this was the Kingdom of Dahomey. Its royal palaces at Abomey have been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1985. Its all-female regiment, the Agojie, is still studied by military historians worldwide. A 30-meter bronze Agojie now stands on the seafront in Cotonou.

Ouidah, on the coast, was one of West Africa's principal slave trading ports. The Door of No Return stands on the beach there, at the end of the old four-kilometer route from the auction square. Benin is also the birthplace of Vodun, which crossed the Atlantic with enslaved Africans and took root in Haiti, Brazil, Cuba, and the American South. Benin recognized it formally in 1996 and marks it with a national holiday on 10 January every year.

Then, the part that most people outside the continent have never heard:

From 19 to 28 February 1990, 488 delegates met at a hotel in Cotonou, declared themselves sovereign, stripped a Marxist-Leninist military ruler of his powers, and wrote a democratic constitution. Freedom House calls it the first conference of its kind in Africa. Gabon, Congo, Mali, Togo, Niger, and Zaire all copied it.

In March 1991, Mathieu Kerekou lost the runoff to Nicephore Soglo and handed over power. He became the first president on mainland Africa to be voted out and leave.

Sixty-six years on, Benin is still asking the question the whole continent is asking. Who gets to choose, and who gets to be heard.

Joyeux anniversaire, Bénin!

Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Freedom House. Pearl T. Robinson, Comparative Studies in Society and History. BBC News. The Brenthurst Foundation. Encyclopaedia Britannica. Global Voices.

text:
So, a bit of history. Morocco in its current form exists because of Islamic imperial expansion over the native Berber population. No current nation in Africa existed in its present form prior to colonisation — borders were drawn by empires, European and otherwise. The Zulus expanded and formed Zululand by conquering neighbouring peoples into their own empire. Conquest and settlement is not, and never has been, a uniquely European phenomenon. Case in point, let us examine some African empires built on conquest and, critically, slavery:

Ashanti Empire (modern Ghana, 1670-1902) — built through military conquest, one of the largest suppliers of slaves to European traders. The Ashanti didn't have slavery imposed on them. They ran a domestic slave economy and actively sold conquered peoples to the Atlantic trade.

Kingdom of Dahomey (modern Benin, 1600-1904) — a military state built on slave-raiding neighbouring peoples. Dahomey was one of the biggest suppliers to the Atlantic slave trade. When the British tried to end the trade, Dahomey's king protested because it was his primary revenue source.

Songhai Empire (1464-1591) — conquered the Mali Empire through military force, controlled trans-Saharan trade routes, maintained a large slave class.

Mali Empire (1235-1600) — expanded through military conquest across West Africa, subjugating numerous peoples.

Islamic empires:

Ottoman Empire (1299-1922) — conquered and occupied the Balkans for over 500 years. Implemented the devshirme system — forcibly taking Christian boys from their families to serve as slave soldiers (Janissaries). Occupied Greece, Serbia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Romania. Ottoman-backed Barbary corsairs raided English, Irish, and European coasts for centuries, enslaving white Europeans who were considered highly valuable.

Arab slave trade — lasted approximately 1,300 years (7th to 20th century), longer than the Atlantic slave trade. An estimated 17-20 million Africans enslaved. Castration of male slaves was routine. Zanzibar was the commercial centre. Saudi Arabia didn't formally abolish slavery until 1962. Mauritania not until 1981. Even now, it's still ongoing.

Umayyad Caliphate (661-750) — at its peak the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from Spain to Central Asia, built entirely through military conquest.

The Ashanti and Dahomey examples are particularly useful because they destroy the "passive African victims of European imperialism" narrative. These were empires that conquered their neighbours and sold them. They weren't bystanders to the slave trade, they were commercial partners in it.

As for Ceuta, it has been under Spanish or Portuguese control since 1415. Before that, it was conquered by Islamic dynasties, and before them, it was Visigothic, Roman, and Carthaginian.

As for Spain, they were occupied by the Moors for 781 years.

I bring all this up because, as Kaur has shown, part of the issue we face is the sheer depth of ignorance displayed by people like herself and her supporters.

Yes! It's an amazing work of art.

Known as the Amazon Monument and Unveiled in Cotonou in the year 2022 by the Government of Benin.  It stands on the Esplanade des Amazones, close to the Atlantic coast.

This giant statue is about 30 meters (98 feet) tall and weighs roughly 150 tons. One of the tallest statues in Africa.

The monument honors the Dahomey Amazons (also called the Agojie), an elite all-female military regiment of the former Kingdom of Dahomey, which occupied much of present-day Benin from the 17th to the late 19th century. These women were renowned for their courage, military discipline, and battlefield skills.

You can also read up and watch the movie "THE WOMAN KING" to know more about the story of the Dahomey female warriors.

text:
The idea that our ancestors never willingly sold slaves to Europeans is a comforting myth that completely collapses when you look at the historical record. It pretends that African societies were passive victims with no political or economic agency, which does a profound disservice to the complexity of the past. In reality, African rulers, warlords, and merchant classes actively participated in the transatlantic slave trade from its earliest days, making calculated decisions to capture and sell human beings in exchange for firearms, textiles, metals, and other goods that consolidated their own power.

Long before Europeans arrived on the coast, slavery and slave trading were already well established across the continent, from the internal servitude systems of various kingdoms to the sprawling trans-Saharan trade that moved millions of Africans into the Islamic world. When Portuguese caravels first appeared in the fifteenth century, they simply plugged into these existing networks. The vast majority of captives who ended up on those ships were not kidnapped by Europeans venturing deep inland; they were marched to coastal forts by African middlemen and sold by African sellers. The Kingdom of Dahomey built an entire militarized state economy around annual slave raids, with the king holding a royal monopoly on the trade at Whydah. Dahomean rulers fiercely resisted British abolitionist pressure well into the nineteenth century because the profits were the backbone of their treasury. Further west, the Ashanti Empire in what is now Ghana expanded its territory through warfare and exported huge numbers of captives to European posts on the Gold Coast, using the imported muskets and ammunition to maintain military dominance over rival groups. The Oyo Empire in Nigeria pushed southwards with its cavalry specifically to acquire slaves for the Atlantic market, controlling the flow through the port of Lagos and growing wealthy from the commerce. Even in the Kingdom of Kongo, where King Afonso I famously protested the destabilizing effects of Portuguese demand in the early 1500s, the trade continued with the active involvement of local nobles and merchants who saw clear material advantages in participating. Inland merchant networks, like the pombeiros in Central Africa, trekked for weeks to bring captives to the coast, and all the profits along the way remained firmly in African hands until the moment of the sale. Pretending these elites were somehow tricked or coerced every single time erases their agency and turns a messy, morally complex history into a simple cartoon of villains and victims drawn along racial lines.

And this willingness to trade in human beings was never confined to one race. If you pull the lens back and look across human history, the grim reality is that virtually every complex society on every continent has practiced slavery and slave trading at some point. The ancient Greeks and Romans took millions of slaves from across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East, selling them in bustling markets that were central to their economies. Viking raiders ran extensive slave routes from the British Isles and along Russian rivers, supplying captives to Byzantium and the Arab world. The Italian city states of Genoa and Venice grew fat on the medieval slave trade, trafficking Slavic people—whose name gave us the word “slave”—from the Black Sea to Egypt and Europe long before the first African was shipped to the Americas. The trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trades under Arab and Berber control stretched over a millennium and transported anywhere from ten to eighteen million Africans across the desert and the sea, while Barbary pirates from North Africa raided European coastal villages and enslaved over a million Europeans as late as the nineteenth century. Moving east, China had massive internal slave markets for millennia, fed by war captives, debtors, and criminals.

text:
People at Queen Victoria’s court whispered about her long before they knew who she was.

The young Black woman appeared at royal events dressed in elegant gowns, moved comfortably among aristocrats, and seemed to enjoy the queen’s personal favor. Some assumed she was secretly adopted. Others spun wilder stories. Few guessed the truth.

She had been born a Yoruba princess in what is now Nigeria. As a child, her kingdom was attacked by the Kingdom of Dahomey, much of her family was killed, and she was taken captive. Contemporary accounts suggest she was destined for ritual sacrifice until British naval officer Captain Frederick Forbes persuaded King Ghezo to release her as a diplomatic gift for Queen Victoria.

Victoria was immediately impressed. She renamed the girl Sarah Forbes Bonetta, combining Forbes’s surname with the ship that carried her to England, and described her as exceptionally intelligent. The queen personally funded her education, followed her life closely, and showed her an unusual degree of affection.

That relationship fueled endless gossip. Why was Queen Victoria so devoted to this young African woman? Some claimed it was politics. Others invented far more scandalous explanations. There is no evidence for those rumors. The queen simply admired Sarah’s intellect, character, and resilience.

When Sarah married the wealthy businessman James Pinson Labulo Davies in 1862, it became one of Victorian London’s most talked-about weddings. The intrigue only deepened when Queen Victoria agreed to become godmother to Sarah’s first daughter.

Sarah died of tuberculosis in 1880 at just 37 years old. The gossip eventually faded, but her story never lost its power. In an empire built on rigid ideas of race and class, an African princess won the respect of Britain’s most powerful woman—and left Victorian society wondering how to explain what they had witnessed.

text:
🔥 22 men were burned alive for their faith. Today, millions walk to that exact spot.

The story of Namugongo Martyrs Shrine 🇺🇬👇

1886 - King Mwanga II executed young Christian converts. 22 Catholics & 23 Anglicans killed between 1885-1887.

1964 - The Martyrs canonized as Saints by Pope Paul VI in Rome.

1967–1975 - The Shrine was built on the exact execution site. Cardinal Nsubuga fundraised globally, Pope Paul VI donated $20,000, with the Vatican adding more. 

Architect Dr. Danhinden designed it like an African hut - 22 copper pillars, 100ft tall.

1993 - Pope John Paul II elevates it to a Minor Basilica.

2015 - A Shs44 billion redevelopment transformed it into a world-class pilgrimage site ahead of Pope Francis' visit - new pavilions, "Martyrs Way" route, and a restored Martyrs' lake.

Today - 1M+ pilgrims flock the shrine every June 3rd. Some walk barefoot from as far as Kenya.

However, this year's celebrations were postponed till further notice.

From a field of ashes to a global pilgrimage site. 🕊️

The painted walls were especially distinctive because they were renewed as part of an annual seasonal cycle. Designs were generally applied during the dry winter months, while summer rains gradually softened or removed them, allowing new compositions to appear the following year. Traditional patterns included chevrons, zigzags, triangles, rectangles, circles, and sharply defined symmetrical forms, using white, black, earth-grey, red ochre, yellow ochre, green, and blue-grey pigments. Ndebele artists also incorporated contemporary imagery inspired by letters, numbers, clocks, buildings, electric lights, plants, and other features of modern life. This combination of inherited geometry and continuing innovation made Ndebele architecture a “dynamic” art—one that preserved cultural continuity while changing with the seasons and reflecting the experiences of each generation.

Source: Walter W. Battiss, The Art of Africa (1958).

Ndebele architecture-united structural design, mural painting, and modeled sculpture into a constantly evolving artistic environment. The villages were organized around enclosed courtyards, entrance passages, decorated gateways, exterior walls, and thatched residential huts.  
 
Men traditionally constructed the huts and walls, incorporating raised forms and sculptural details that anticipated the painted decoration later applied by women. Gateways, portals, and entrance posts were often shaped into elaborate works of abstract clay sculpture, with sunlight and shadow strengthening their three-dimensional appearance. The architecture was therefore more than functional shelter: the walls, entrances, and courtyards formed a coordinated artistic composition in which construction, sculpture, and painting worked together.

The painted walls were especially distinctive because they were renewed as part of an annual seasonal cycle. Designs were generally applied during the dry winter months, while summer rains gradually softened or removed them, allowing new compositions to appear the following year. Traditional patterns included chevrons, zigzags, triangles, rectangles, circles, and sharply defined symmetrical forms, using white, black, earth-grey, red ochre, yellow ochre, green, and blue-grey pigments. Ndebele artists also incorporated contemporary imagery inspired by letters, numbers, clocks, buildings, electric lights, plants, and other features of modern life. This combination of inherited geometry and continuing innovation made Ndebele architecture a “dynamic” art—one that preserved cultural continuity while changing with the seasons and reflecting the experiences of each generation.

Source: Walter W. Battiss, The Art of Africa (1958).

In the terminology of the book, “cult shrine” means a religious institution devoted to a particular deity or spiritual power; it is not necessarily being used in the modern negative sense of the word “cult.”

The accompanying text explains that the abosom, or Akan divinities, have specially trained priests and priestesses who serve in their shrines. These religious specialists are believed to:

1.) Understand the language of the gods; 

2.) Interpret divine communications for worshippers; 

3.) Present human needs and requests to the gods;and, on some occasions, influence the gods to respond favourably to human wishes. 

The caption on page 67 explicitly identifies the decorations as  Akan symbolic murals representing:

1.) The  ram’s horn, and the Sankofa bird.

These designs were not merely ornamental. Elsewhere, the book explains that Akan artists used proverbial images as a form of pictographic communication. Similar symbols appeared on clan vessels, funerary sculptures, cult shrines, Kente and Adinkra textiles, drums, gold weights and linguist staffs. They embodied religious, historical and philosophical statements that knowledgeable viewers could interpret.

text:
Ashanti architecture belongs on the top 10 list of the most sophisticated and beautiful traditional African architectural styles.

The houses were built with timber frames covered in mud plaster, steep thatched roofs, elevated floors, and richly decorated walls filled with symbolic designs. These motifs were one of the most distinctive features of Asante architecture. They were not merely decorative; they carried symbolic, philosophical, religious, and cultural meanings.

Sadly, most Asante towns, including Kumasi, were devastated during the long wars against the British in the nineteenth century. Many palaces, public buildings, and elite residences were destroyed and never rebuilt in their original form. After the wars, Asante society gradually moved away from the old architectural tradition.

For anyone interested in learning more about Ashanti architecture, I recommend reading Asante Traditional Buildings (2021 Edition), Ghana Museums and Monuments Board & UNESCO. Foreword by Otumfuo Osei Tutu II. Published under the UNESCO World Heritage programme.

text:
22 June in History

1652
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
A severe windstorm raged throughout the night.
Van Riebeeck wrote, somewhat tongue-in-cheek, that he was surprised everyone was still alive the next morning and had not been blown away.
The yacht was also, remarkably, still at anchor.
Concern had been expressed, however, regarding the skipper of the yacht, who had sent out a distress signal with a lamp late the previous evening.
Further inquiry revealed that he had merely been seeking assistance with an exceptionally large quantity of fish that had been caught in a net.
Exactly how this was accomplished during such a storm was not recorded.

1653
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Dawn brought a gloomy, overcast day with constant rain and wind. The wind blew steadily from the northwest.

Sunday, 22 June 1654
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
A lovely sunny day.
Jan Danielssen, the man who had threatened to kill Van Riebeeck and cut off the ears of some of the other officials, was sentenced on this day.
According to the sentence, he was to be keelhauled, placed in chains for six months, and forfeit three months' wages.

1655
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak brought a warm and pleasant day at the Cape, with no noteworthy incidents.

1656
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
As with the previous few days, daybreak was warm and pleasant.
During the night, the Kaapmans, an indigenous group, stole twelve ox hides that had been stretched out to dry for later use.
The sergeant of the garrison was ordered to visit Harry's people and demand the return of the hides. If Harry failed to comply, some of his cattle were to be confiscated.
Harry quickly produced the hides, but it was too late, as they had already been cut up.
Harry then requested an audience during the afternoon, during which he intended to hand over the culprits.
He kept his word and arrived at the fort later that day. According to him, however, the guilty parties had simply disappeared.
Harry apologized for the behaviour of his people and asked that they be forgiven this one time. Van Riebeeck agreed.

1657
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Diary entries from 19 to 23 June 1657 were recorded together.
The days are described as overcast with intermittent rain. No noteworthy incidents are mentioned.

1658
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
No mention is made of the weather.
The Fiscal and a detachment of soldiers were sent before dawn to the free burgher settlements.
They were instructed to investigate rumours that livestock were being slaughtered and sold to ships. They were also to determine exactly how much land had been cultivated and what crops had been planted.
Their primary task, however, was to bring the slave who had been captured the previous day back to the fort for questioning.
Harry and several prominent Kaapman chiefs arrived at the fort during the day to discuss the escaped slaves.
Van Riebeeck took two men, Schacher and Pieter Otegno, into custody. They were informed that they were being detained because they had sheltered and assisted the runaway slaves. They would be released once the slaves were handed over.
Anthony ("Doman"), mentioned the previous day, nearly exploded with anger and accused Eva of being responsible.
Van Riebeeck and the others denied his accusations.
Reading between the lines, it appears that Van Riebeeck was already considering sending Anthony back to Batavia.
A resolution was also adopted that day. Steven Janssen and Hendrik Boom were elected to serve on the council responsible for matters concerning the free burghers.
For Janssen, it was his second term in the position.

Sunday, 22 June 1659
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The weather is described as pleasant, with the wind still blowing from the south-southeast.
The twelve delegates departed before dawn to visit the Cochoqua people. Six oxen pulled their wagon, and Eva accompanied them.
Gifts were sent to Oedasoa, the chief.
The Fiscal and an armed escort accompanied the delegation as far as the Brack River.

1835
From the recollections of the Voortrekker J.H. Hattingh.
Hattingh writes that Captain Adam Kok's community was the first they encountered.
According to Hattingh, the missionary Archbell lived among the community and had established a mission station there.
(The author notes that Hattingh's memory appears to have failed him here. Historical records indicate that the first indigenous group encountered by the Voortrekkers were the Barolong people at Moroka's Hoek, Blesberg.)
Hattingh further writes that Hendrik Potgieter concluded a peace treaty with Kok (or more correctly, Moroka).
The people were reportedly pleased to see the Voortrekkers because Mzilikazi ("Moselekatse") had killed or carried off many of their people, and they believed peace would now prevail.
Hattingh records that they welcomed the Voortrekkers with open arms and that some of the trekkers hunted game for them to eat.

Thursday, 22 June 1837
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Carolus was already burning charcoal early in the morning, probably for use in the forge.
Albach and Low were occupied building a school for the children.
Pieta spent the day in the veld cutting reeds and bulrushes. He returned around four o'clock in the afternoon with a heavily loaded wagon.
Mrs. Scheepers (Antjie) and Botha had, according to Louis, completed their rondavels neatly.
Jan had also built a rondavel, which Louis described as resembling a wagon tent.
Later that afternoon, a very elderly indigenous man arrived with several women.
The old man carried a cooking pot with one broken leg, while the women brought pumpkins and beans they wished to barter.

Thursday, 22 June 1837
From the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.
The Reverend spent the day preparing a sermon.
He also drafted a written invitation regarding the forthcoming Communion service and distributed it to all the wagon camps.

Friday, 22 June 1838
From the diary of Reverend Erasmus Smit.
(Entries for 20 and 21 June are missing from the diary.)
News reached the camp that Mrs. A. Greyling had given birth to a healthy son at about nine o'clock the previous evening.
Reverend Smit wrote that they praised and thanked the Lord for this blessing.

General Christiaan de Wet launched attacks against the railway north of Kroonstad across a broad front.

General Smith-Dorrien announced that he had destroyed eleven farmhouses in a single day after the telegraph line between the Renoster River and Heuningspruit had been damaged.
Major H. de la Gough arrived in and occupied Standerton.

President Marthinus Theunis Steyn issued a proclamation to both republics and all burghers in the field.

Carel Boshoff, a member of General Beyers's commando and renowned marksman, reportedly shot and killed Lieutenant A.C.G. Besley at a distance recorded as approximately 1,200 metres near Alma, not far from Nylstroom.

The first Chinese mine workers arrived in South Africa to work on the gold mines.
Their recruitment was largely promoted by Alfred Milner and others.
This temporarily solved the demand for inexpensive unskilled labour.
Within a year, approximately 34,000 Chinese labourers were in the country.
When Milner returned to England in 1907, the repatriation of Chinese workers also began, and by 1910 the last of them had left South Africa.

1915
The Rebellion
General Christiaan Rudolph de Wet, one of South Africa's most prominent military leaders, was convicted of high treason in the Bloemfontein Supreme Court.
He was fined £2,000 and sentenced to six years' imprisonment.
De Wet pleaded not guilty to treason but guilty to what he described as rebellion.
The fine, a very substantial amount by contemporary standards, was paid within four months through the "General De Wet Half-Crown Fund," established by Het Volksblad.

text:
MEMORIES OF PONTE CITY; IMBALI FLATS & EASTMOOR CRESCENT UMHLANGA

Years ago, when I first arrived in Johannesburg, I squatted at Ponte City in Berea — back when it was still in its prime. Tenpin bowling in the basement, a laundromat on site, and we were there thanks to connections with staff from the Transkei consulate. Those were wild days.

Party weekends often meant heading to the residence of Bhut’ Mncedisi Philiso in Waterkloof, Pretoria. That’s where I first met Zinzi Mandela… and, funnily enough, Dumile Mateza was on the decks as the DJ.

From Ponte City, I moved to High Point in Hillbrow, then to Imbali Flats in Berea. All of them were still pristine back then.But here’s where I really messed up.

One weekend we drove out to Lonehill after seeing pamphlets in the Sunday papers advertising off-plan cluster developments. I spoke to an agent from Zotos Construction who told me, “The property market is the ultimate barometer — investing in bricks and mortar is one of the smartest things you can do.” The clusters were sparse, the prices were ridiculously low. But I was young and foolish. I thought, “That’s what older people do.”

So instead, I wasted hundreds of thousands of rands on rent over the years. Even after moving to Durban, the pattern continued. I stayed at Kalbarri Court in Umngeni near the Bird Park, then Eastmoor Crescent in Umhlanga/La Lucia so the kids could be close to Atholton Primary. That same Eastmoor house — which was on the market for well under a million back then — recently popped up on TV, converted into sea-facing luxury apartments selling for millions each. 

The little place I rented in Umdloti at The Cascades in Bellamont Road? Now it’s on Airbnb. Those units were going for just under R100k off-plan at the time.

The only apartment I’ve never regretted buying is the tiny one at Club Blues on Grayston Drive in Sandton — occupied around the time Jacqui Mogokeng became Miss South Africa. It was so small you could jump from the bedroom door straight onto the bed. Even the rondavel at my granny’s homestead in Tsomo felt bigger!

But here’s the lesson I learned, the hard way: You’re never too young to start investing. Property, in particular, has a way of rewarding those who get in early. Don’t wait for “older people” money. 

Start where you are, with what you have. The future version of you will thank you. The property prices on the Atlantic Seaboard and generally across the Western Cape, are of course a cause for concern as they are skyrocketing so high, there's a huge fraction of society that will never ever smell property there. 

That is why it's so important to look out for properties at auctions, form viable property stokvels and invest in farms and fixed properties in general rather than remaining enslaved to landlords. 

This reminds me of Sandhurst Estate which at the time, was the most expensive residential estate in South Africa. Developed by Bakos Properties with the show house furnished by them. Oh my goodness! I swooned over the pastel hues, the perspex furniture. The Caribbean flamingos and the rockery and calming water at the entrance. Classical music played softly in the background throughout the show unit from petite Bang & Olufsen [I think], speakers. It was ultra-luxurious and how wealthy one would've been today.

What’s one investment lesson life taught you the hard way? Drop it in the comments.
